radish.1: Raphanus sativus. Ready in half a minute, which makes it the most impatient vegetable I've ever catalogued.
radish.3: Tobias wrote 'good for snacking while waiting for other things' next to this entry. Scientifically accurate.
radish.5: You have grown more radishes than the rest of Bramblewick combined. Pip wants to know if you'll sell him a sack.
radish.7: I've started a radish growth chart. It is very short and very crowded.
radish.10: A gold-leaf page for the humble radish. It earned every flake.

carrot.1: Daucus carota. Pull gently from the shoulders. Moss will try to help. Moss will not help.
carrot.3: Carrots taste sweeter after a long wait in cool soil. Yours are not waiting long, and are still very good.
carrot.5: Juniper says carrots are the only crop she can draw from memory. She's drawn about forty of yours.
carrot.7: The almanac's carrot page now has more jam stains than writing. I'm blaming Tobias retroactively.
carrot.10: Gold border, carrot page. Moss has been informed and is very proud of himself for some reason.

lettuce.1: Lactuca sativa. Crisp, leafy, and mostly water. A bit like Ziggy's promises.
lettuce.3: Picked at the right moment, a lettuce squeaks. I'm told this is not a normal thing to listen for.
lettuce.5: Goldie's sandwiches have improved noticeably since you started growing lettuce in volume.
lettuce.7: I pressed one of your lettuce leaves in the almanac. It took up four pages.
lettuce.10: The lettuce page goes gold. I didn't expect to feel this strongly about a salad.

strawberry.1: Fragaria × ananassa. The seeds are on the outside. Nobody has ever explained to me why.
strawberry.3: Tobias's jam stains are mostly strawberry. Mystery solved, though not the mystery of why he read with jam.
strawberry.5: Your strawberries keep showing up in Pip's tarts. Do not tell him I told you he hides the best ones.
strawberry.7: A bee on your strawberry patch visited eleven flowers while I watched. I had nowhere else to be.
strawberry.10: Strawberry, gold-leafed. Tobias would want this page framed. With jam on it, probably.

wheat.1: Triticum aestivum. Ten thousand years of farmers have stood where you're standing, watching it sway.
wheat.3: Rufus says the mill wheel turns happier with your wheat. He refuses to explain what 'happier' means.
wheat.5: Bramblewick hasn't milled this much flour since before the wheel jammed.
wheat.7: Stand in your wheat on a windy day and you'll hear it whisper. Or that's Moss. Check for Moss.
wheat.10: Wheat earns its gold page. Fitting: it's practically the colour already.

tomato.1: Solanum lycopersicum. Botanically a fruit, culinarily a vegetable, and personally my favourite argument.
tomato.3: A ripe tomato should feel heavy for its size. Yours feel heavy for their size and also slightly smug.
tomato.5: Bruno puts your tomatoes on everything. Everything. I've seen him put one on a pastry.
tomato.7: I've counted the seeds in one of your tomatoes for the record. It was a slow afternoon. 214.
tomato.10: The tomato page goes gold, and the fruit-versus-vegetable debate stays closed in this book.

corn.1: Zea mays. Every strand of silk is attached to one kernel. Every single one. Go and look.
corn.3: Corn grows so fast in summer you can almost hear it creak. Almost. I've tried.
corn.5: Pip has started a popcorn experiment with your corn. The bakery smells wonderful and slightly alarming.
corn.7: Your corn is tall enough now that I lost Juniper in it for twenty minutes.
corn.10: Gold border for corn. I'm told the scarecrow is jealous.

potato.1: Solanum tuberosum. Same family as the tomato, which explains nothing and everything.
potato.3: Every potato you dig is a little surprise. Some of yours have faces. I've named three.
potato.5: Goldie says your potatoes are why the store's soup sells out by noon.
potato.7: A potato can regrow a whole plant from one eye. Resilient. Rather like this farm.
potato.10: The potato page goes gold. I've moved my three named potatoes onto it as witnesses.

blueberry.1: Vaccinium corymbosum. The blue is in a waxy bloom on the skin. Rub it off and they look almost black.
blueberry.3: Blueberries want acid soil. Yours don't seem to care. I've stopped arguing with your soil.
blueberry.5: Nell says your blueberries make the best bait she's ever been too fond of to use.
blueberry.7: Juniper painted your blueberry bushes and ran out of blue. She had to send to the city for more.
blueberry.10: Blueberry, gold-leafed. The page is very blue and very gold. I approve.

pumpkin.1: Cucurbita pepo. Starts as a flower, ends as furniture.
pumpkin.3: Your pumpkins are getting big enough that Bruno has started measuring them with a tape.
pumpkin.5: Somebody carved a face into one of your pumpkins overnight. My money is on Ziggy.
pumpkin.7: The pumpkin vines have crept two plots over. They're ambitious. I respect that in a squash.
pumpkin.10: The pumpkin page goes gold. It's also the heaviest page in the almanac, somehow.

sunflower.1: Helianthus annuus. Young flowers follow the sun across the sky. Old ones just face east and wait.
sunflower.3: Each sunflower head is hundreds of tiny flowers in a spiral. Count the spirals. Actually, don't. It takes hours.
sunflower.5: The bees have voted. Your sunflowers are the best address in Bramblewick.
sunflower.7: Pip toasts your sunflower seeds. The whole street knows when he does.
sunflower.10: Gold page for the sunflower. It finally has something as bright as it is.

cotton.1: Gossypium hirsutum. The fluff is the seed's way of hitching a ride. Clever plant.
cotton.3: Cotton bolls split open when they're ready, like they're showing off.
cotton.5: Bramblewick's quilts have been patched with your cotton. Mine included. Thank you.
cotton.7: A field of open cotton looks like snow that forgot what season it is.
cotton.10: The cotton page goes gold. I pressed a boll into the corner for softness.

grapes.1: Vitis vinifera. Some vines live for over a century. Plan accordingly.
grapes.3: Grapes ripen in clusters, never all at once. They're as patient as you've had to be.
grapes.5: Rufus has been 'testing' your grapes. Daily. In quantity. For science, he says.
grapes.7: Your vines have started to twist into shapes. One looks like Tobias. I may be tired.
grapes.10: Grape page, gold border. Tobias always said a good vine outlives its farmer. This one will outlive the almanac.

coffee.1: Coffea arabica. A cherry, not a bean. Every cup in town starts as fruit on your farm.
coffee.3: Coffee takes a whole day to ripen and about four seconds to drink. Bruno has opinions on this ratio.
coffee.5: Nell claims she can taste which plot your coffee came from. I've tested her. She can't.
coffee.7: The almanac's coffee page is the only one without jam on it. Tobias drank his black, apparently.
coffee.10: Coffee, gold-leafed. I'd celebrate, but I'm already on my third cup.

golden_melon.1: Cucumis aureus. Not in any book but this one. Tobias found the first seed in a hollow log, he says. I have doubts.
golden_melon.3: Two days in the ground and still worth every hour. The Golden Moth agrees.
golden_melon.5: You've grown more golden melons than I thought existed. I may need to revise 'rare'.
golden_melon.7: Hold a golden melon to your ear. You won't hear anything. But everybody tries.
golden_melon.10: The golden melon gets a gold page. Redundant? Perhaps. Deserved? Absolutely.

later: Still growing. Still counting. Still impressed, and I don't impress easily.
I've run out of margin on this page. I'm writing on the next one. You've earned two pages.
At this point the crop knows you better than I do.
Tobias wrote 'patience is a farming tool' on the inside cover. You've worn that tool smooth.
Another milestone. I'll need a bigger almanac.
The numbers on this page are getting silly. Good silly.
